drills.q: Name two things agents are genuinely good at in architecture review.
drills.a: Consistency checks across a large codebase against a stated invariant, and missing-case enumeration against a contract (also: drafting and drift detection).

drills.q: Why can't an agent judge whether a tradeoff is right for a specific org?
drills.a: That judgment depends on institutional memory (past outages, political compromises, customer contracts) never written down anywhere the agent could be shown.

drills.q: Which ADR field must always require a named human, and why not agent-filled?
drills.a: The Decision field -- it's the one place the org's actual judgment must appear, attributed to someone accountable for it.

drills.q: Name the failure mode of agent-generated design docs from an existing codebase.
drills.a: Confident-description drift -- describing what the code looks like it does rather than what it actually does, with equal fluency whether right or wrong.

drills.q: Why is a model reviewing its own design output a weak check?
drills.a: It checks whether the design looks like the kind of thing generated correctly, not whether it matches reality -- the same weights rationalize the same shortcut twice.

drills.q: What three properties define an effective adversarial design review?
drills.a: A different model family, no shared reasoning context (read-only, cold), and 'enumerate every failure mode' framing instead of an approve/reject verdict.

drills.q: How do you mechanically check a design doc against real code?
drills.a: Extract every checkable claim, locate the implementing code, report match/mismatch with file+line evidence, and track unverifiable claims as a separate category from confirmed matches.

drills.q: Why must 'could not verify' never collapse into 'matches' in a drift checker?
drills.a: It reintroduces the confident-description failure the check exists to catch, one layer up -- a false confirmation is worse than an honest unverified flag.

drills.q: What's the estimated annual documentation-drift cost for a 50-person engineering team, and why does it compound under agent-assisted development?
drills.a: Upward of $200K/year; commit velocity is higher with agent assistance, so more surface area drifts, faster.

drills.q: State the accountability line for AI-assisted architecture review in one sentence.
drills.a: The agent does not own the decision, at any point in the pipeline, regardless of how good its draft was -- this is a governance requirement, not a capability gap that better models fix.

drills.q: Is a bot that auto-approves PRs conforming to accepted ADRs a complete review solution?
drills.a: No -- it's reliable for mechanical conformance but can't judge whether the underlying ADR itself still holds; that still needs periodic human review with institutional context.

drills.q: If two different models independently agree a design is sound, how much should that weigh?
drills.a: Less than it sounds -- both may share a systematic blind spot in how models reason about that problem class. It's evidence to weigh, not a decision made automatically.
